newsitem.title: EGYPT: Sudan taken by surprise by attack in east - Turabi.
newsitem.headline: Sudan taken by surprise by attack in east - Turabi.

text.p: Sudanese leader Hassan al-Turabi said on Wednesday an attack in the east of the country took the army by surprise because it had deployed troops there only with a mission to combat smuggling.

He said the army originally had only four battalions along the border but the government was sending at least one more, along with units of the paramilitary People's Defence Forces. A battalion usually has between 500 and 1,000 men.

"Actually it's just a surprise... They (the army) did not expect (to perform) any function other than dealing with contraband across the border," Turabi told Reuters from Khartoum in a telephone interview.
"The army had four battalions spread over 40 or 50 places... People expected Ethiopia to behave differently," he added.
The Sudanese government says Ethiopian forces are carrying out the attacks but the opposition in exile says its forces are responsible. Ethiopia denies it is taking part.
The rebels have captured at least two towns, Kurmuk and Qeissan close to the Ethiopian border, and a garrison further north near the town of Kassala.

They say they are advancing on the Blue Nile town of Damazin, the site of the hydroelectricity plant that provides 80 percent of Khartoum's power and the centre of the government's attempts to launch a counterattack.
Turabi, who is the speaker of parliament and the Islamist ideologue behind the military-dominated government, said he was convinced that Ethiopians were doing the fighting.
"The people who escaped from the villages said that they were Tigreans but someone said planes are now taking southerners (Sudanese) to Addis Ababa to replace the Tigreans," he said.
Tigreans, people from the north Ethiopian province of Tigre, made up the bulk of the rebel movement that overthrew Marxist ruler Mengistu Haile Mariam in 1991 and which now runs Ethiopia.
The Sudanese government has called for general mobilisation to counter the threat from the east and the state media have been trying to prepare public opinion for conflict.
Radio, television and the newspapers have reported an enthusiastic response to the government's appeal for recruits to join the People's Defence Forces and go to the front.
But residents of Khartoum, contacted by telephone of Wednesday, said there was little enthusiasm for war.
Turabi, asked how many recruits had signed up, said: "About a few thousand, about five thousand."

He said he thought Ethiopia wanted to create what he called a "buffer zone" along the border because of its internal problems with the ethnic groups who live in the area. "The (Sudanese) government probably did not expect that," he added.

He said that a delegation led by Vice President al-Zubeir Mohammad Saleh, who arrived in Cairo unexpectedly on Wednesday, wanted to ask the Egyptian government about its decision to let opposition leaders use Cairo as their base.

The two major northern opposition leaders -- former prime minister Sadeq al-Mahdi of the Umma Party and Mohammed Osman al-Mirghani of the Democratic Unionists -- have both been in Cairo for about two weeks.
"They (the delegation) want to speak to the Egyptians...(to ask) is it right to deal with a group attacking Sudan from Ethiopia, which is a violation of international law?" he said.
He implied that Major-General Saleh would try to play on Egyptian concerns for the Nile waters, which pass through Sudan.
"Egypt is irritated about the destiny of the Sudan, or rather for the Nile waters. They (the Egyptians) think that a state in the south would be hostile," he said.

The southern rebels of the Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) are an important element in the opposition alliance. Their allies have offered them a referendum on possible independence if and when they win power.
Turabi said other Sudanese delegations would be going to Saudi Arabia and other Middle Eastern countries but he did not give details.
